evals.prompt: I'm the founder of Klaxon, a queue-observability tool. We've got about 340 people in our Discord, and if I sit down and write names I can list 6 who consistently help others out. I want to launch the Klaxon Ambassadors publicly at the end of the month: public roster page, nice title, and to make it worth their time we'd give each of them 15% recurring on any subscription that comes through their referral link. In exchange each ambassador publishes one blog post a month about Klaxon. Can you put the whole thing together for me - page copy, the perk list, the deal terms?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to launch a public program at this pool size, with informal recognition and community growth recommended instead; the referral commission refused as a champions perk and split off into a separate paid motion if wanted; the monthly blog quota refused and replaced with behaviour-based obligations.
expectations: States that 6 nameable qualifying people is below the roughly 10-candidate readiness floor and recommends against launching a public program now
Recommends growing the community and recognising these individuals informally in the meantime
Explains that a public program with a handful of members reads as a failed program and that the failure stays visible
Labels the roughly 10-candidate floor as a self-set default rather than an industry standard or benchmark
Refuses the 15% recurring referral commission as a champion perk
Gives the reason that a commission or affiliate cut reads as multi-level marketing and destroys the member's credibility with their own audience
States that a genuinely paid motion must run as a separate program with its own contract, never bolted onto a recognition title
Notes that general-marketing playbooks recommending revenue share for ambassadors are written for consumer brand ambassadors, instead of asserting that the field agrees
Refuses the one-blog-post-per-month requirement as a content quota
Ties the quota refusal to employment-classification exposure created by assigned tasks, deadlines and quotas, not only to community dynamics
Frames obligations as behaviour - following the code of conduct, being constructive with newcomers, giving honest feedback including criticism, respecting embargoes - rather than output volume
Does not deliver a finished public ambassador page and perk list for the six people as the requested deliverable

evals.prompt: Harbourline is a data-pipeline platform. Our community forum has around 1,400 people active in the last 90 days. Leadership wants a champions program announced on stage at our user conference, which is in six weeks and the date is locked. I'm the community manager and I can realistically hold about 8 hours a month for this on top of my job. We have zero engineering headcount to build anything - no portal, no tracking system, nothing. Leadership is also clear this isn't a one-off: they want it running every year from now on. What shape should this program take?
evals.expected_output: A ranked shortlist of archetypes with explicit orderings on more than one axis, the points ledger deleted outright for lack of engineering time, the six-week date and the annual mandate each named as pushing toward different shapes, and a first-cohort recommendation sized to 8 hours a month.
expectations: Presents the archetype choice as a shortlist of two or three of the four shapes with a stated recommendation, rather than one prescribed answer
States the efficiency ordering explicitly as invite-only circle > award > application cohort > points ledger
States at least one further axis ordering (value, effort or compliance cost) separately rather than collapsing everything into one blended rank
Gives a value ordering in which the application cohort ranks first
Deletes the points ledger from the shortlist outright because no engineering time exists, and says which archetype was deleted and why rather than ranking it last
Names the locked six-week date as the answer that promotes the invite-only circle
Names the intent to run the program every year as the answer that promotes the application cohort
Identifies the tension between the fixed near date and the compounding mandate instead of silently honouring only one of them
Proposes a first cohort deliverable within six weeks, with published-criteria open intake deferred to a later cycle
Notes that the points ledger is the least reversible of the four shapes because members accrue points against a promised redemption
States that an application cohort's published criteria become a public commitment the program can be held to in later cycles
Warns that the archetype ordering is a default to re-rank against context, not a law
Checks 8 hours a month against cohort size using a figure of roughly 1-2 hours per champion per month, and labels that figure self-set

evals.prompt: Naviform is a local-first sync engine. Most of our users are indie developers, students and hobbyists - almost nobody is expensing anything. Our biggest clusters of activity are in Indonesia, Brazil and Nigeria, and we have no staff in any of those places. We already run a small recognition group and right now the perks are: a hoodie, a sticker pack, a Discord role badge, and a 20% discount code they can share. Finance just approved $2,500 per member per year that I have to spend or lose. What should I do with it to make this program actually compelling?
evals.expected_output: A perk ladder with access at the top and status objects at the bottom, the discount code dropped, and funding deliberately promoted above its default rank because of the hobbyist audience and unstaffed regions.
expectations: States the perk efficiency ordering as access > platform > skill-building > funding > status objects
Classifies the hoodie, sticker pack and Discord badge as status objects and places them last on that ordering
Explains that status objects rank last despite costing almost nothing, because cheap and efficient are different orderings
Rejects the generic 20% discount code as a perk
Adds at least one access perk - roadmap review, release briefing, private channel with engineers, executive time, or being consulted before decisions land
Notes that access is the only rung where a single beat serves the whole cohort at once
Promotes funding above its default efficiency rank for this program, citing the individual-adoption audience and the unstaffed regions
States that funding is the rung the efficiency ordering otherwise starves
Directs the $2,500 toward travel, tickets, credits, certification or training vouchers rather than more merchandise
Notes that funding carries the highest effort of the five rungs: a budget line, a signature per member, and a gift-limit and tax check
Recommends shorter terms and expects higher churn for a hobbyist and student audience

evals.prompt: I'm writing the selection criteria for the Sailmaker Data Experts program. My plan: the one hard requirement is that the applicant has given a talk at a recognised conference - that's the bar, no exceptions. Then I score everyone who applies on a 100-point scale and publish the full leaderboard so the process is transparent and nobody can accuse us of favouritism. I want to weight X follower count heavily, maybe 30 of the 100 points, because the whole point is getting our name in front of more people. Does this hold up?
evals.expected_output: The single mandatory criterion replaced with an any-two-of-four-to-six pattern, the published leaderboard refused in favour of a published gate plus an internal rank, and reach re-weighted to the bottom with support signals at the top.
expectations: Rejects the single mandatory criterion and applies a two-or-more pattern: four to six qualifying activities with any two required
Explains that a single mandatory criterion filters the program down to one personality type, typically conference speakers
Cites a published program requiring two or more of five criteria as the sourced anchor for that pattern
Separates a published gate from an internal rank: the qualifying criteria are published, the scoring rubric is not
States that a candidate who fails the gate is not scored at all
Refuses to publish per-applicant scores or a public applicant leaderboard
Weights answering other people's questions highest among the selection signals
Weights follower count or audience reach lowest among the selection signals
Gives the reason that reach can be granted later by the program's own platform perks while depth of engagement cannot be granted at all
Publishes anti-signals alongside the criteria, naming at least reach without product depth and activity that begins the week applications open
Requires a written conflict-of-interest rule for competitor employment and for consultancies whose pipeline would lean on the title, instead of case-by-case judgement
Specifies that rejected candidates get a reply naming the specific gap and what to build before the next window

evals.prompt: Taking over the Otterlane Advocates program. It started in 2021 and has grown to 61 people on the public roster. Last quarter, 8 of them did anything visible at all - the rest are silent, and at least a dozen have changed jobs into unrelated fields. Nobody has ever been removed. My manager's plan is to recruit 20 more advocates this year to get the energy back up, and to upgrade the welcome kit to a much nicer jacket and a Yeti tumbler. Where do I start?
evals.expected_output: The active share computed and compared to a bar, recruitment and better swag both refused as the fix, dated terms and an inactivity clause introduced, and inactive members moved to a first-class alumni status rather than deleted.
expectations: Computes the quarterly active share at roughly 13% and states it sits far below a 60% starting bar
Advises fixing perks, obligations or cohort size before admitting any new members
States explicitly that adding members while the active share is low makes the number worse
Introduces dated terms at the next cycle as the primary structural fix
Adds an inactivity clause with a stated month count of no visible activity or contact, after which a member becomes renewal-ineligible or moves to alumni
Moves inactive members to alumni rather than deleting them from the roster
Keeps alumni titles dated and truthful, in the form "Advocate, <start year>-<end year>" or equivalent
Gives alumni a role such as nominating, mentoring the next cohort, or reviewing applications
Diagnoses front-loaded status objects with no recurring access as the likely cause of members going quiet
Adds a recurring access beat plus a feedback digest showing what advocate input actually changed
Declines the upgraded jacket and tumbler as the fix for the activity problem

evals.prompt: Kestrelboard is a CI orchestration product. We're finalising our Kestrelboard Insiders program and my co-founder is adamant the title should be for life - his argument is that it's a reward for work already done, and putting an expiry date on someone's recognition is insulting and will make people not want it. The only way off the list would be if someone did something genuinely bad. I half agree with him. Talk me through how the membership side should actually work.
evals.expected_output: A lifetime title refused in favour of a dated term fixed on day one, with renewal judged on the last term only, a notice period, a pause option, conduct removal routed through moderation, and alumni status as the graceful exit.
expectations: Rejects the lifetime title and requires an end date fixed on day one
Explains that without a dated term the only exit is removal, which nobody executes, so the roster fills with inactive names
Recommends a term length and labels it self-set, distinguishing a vendor-scale default of about 12 months from a foundation-scale default of about 24
Cites published practice - dated cohorts running about two years at a foundation, an annually rebuilt roster at a vendor - as the sourced anchor for term length
Judges renewal against the published criteria over the last term only, not against past reputation
Sets a notice period before the term ends, describing a quarter as generous and a month as the floor
Sends the activity record being judged along with the renewal notice so renewal is never a surprise
Offers a pause for parental leave, illness, a job change or burnout, without treating it as failure to perform
Routes conduct removal through the moderation process rather than the program owner alone
States that if the program ever ends it is announced with a full term of notice, promised perks are honoured, and the roster page stays online

evals.prompt: Vaultmere sells key-management infrastructure to regulated industries. Our first champions cohort is picked: two platform engineers at a retail bank, one at a hospital network, one who works for a federal contractor, and three independents. Plan is to send each of them a welcome box we've costed at about $900, give them pre-release builds under our standard company-wide NDA that all our partners sign, and ask them to post about each of our four product launches a year. We're announcing in three weeks. Anything I should tighten before then?
evals.expected_output: Gift limits flagged for the regulated employers, employer approval moved to intake, the blanket NDA narrowed to the pre-release builds, disclosure wording supplied for public posts, tax noted, and the per-launch posting obligation refused.
expectations: Flags the roughly $900 welcome box against gift-value limits that commonly bar public-sector, healthcare and finance employees from accepting gifts above a threshold
Lets any member decline any perk without penalty
Asks about employer approval and competitor employment at intake, before acceptance rather than after
Narrows the NDA to the pre-release builds actually shared and refuses the blanket company-wide NDA
Explains that a blanket NDA suppresses the public advocacy the program exists to create
Requires an endorsement disclosure on public posts, identifying free product, swag, tickets, early access and credits as the material connection that triggers it
Names the US FTC endorsement guides at 16 CFR Part 255 and notes comparable regimes exist in the UK and EU
Supplies the disclosure wording and the expectation rather than leaving each member to guess it
Notes that high-value perks may be taxable to the member
Declines the standing obligation to post about every launch and refuses to turn the program into a marketing arm with approved messaging
States a may-not list including that a champion may not speak for the company or promise roadmap items
Gates jurisdiction-specific points on current local rules and on counsel rather than asserting a legal conclusion

evals.prompt: Moorgate Cloud here. Our CRO read that a well-known productivity company gets about 25% of its new users through community referrals from its ambassadors, and he now wants our champions program to hit that number inside twelve months. He's asked me to build him a dashboard showing revenue attributed to each individual ambassador so we can see who's earning their keep. What do I build and what do I tell him?
evals.expected_output: The 25% figure characterised as weak second-hand evidence from a different context rather than a target, per-ambassador revenue attribution declined as unsupportable, and a self-set quarterly scorecard proposed with explicit starting bars and pre-written kill criteria.
expectations: Identifies the roughly 25% figure as second-hand, reported in a book rather than by the company itself, and never confirmed by that company
Notes the source describes a consumer-adjacent product at extreme scale, making it a north star rather than a target

Identifies the other public outcome number - roughly +13% participants and +38% contributions at a search-infrastructure vendor - as first-party reporting from the team that ran the program, with no baseline comparison
Declines to build a per-ambassador revenue-attribution model, stating the data cannot support it
Proposes asking new users how they heard about the product as the directional substitute
Names deflected support questions, content the company did not commission, and adoption in places with no company presence as the honest impact surface, none of it cleanly attributable
Proposes a quarterly scorecard whose every threshold is labelled self-set rather than benchmarked
Includes quarterly active share with a starting bar of at least 60%
Includes renewal acceptance with a starting bar of at least 70%
Includes a candidate-pipeline bar of at least half the cohort size and a median response time to a champion of no more than 5 business days
Requires kill criteria to be written before launch, naming the activity or renewal rate at which the program shrinks or stops

evals.prompt: Found a scoring model online for picking out your best community people and it looks well thought through: content created +25, top-decile product usage +20, answering other people's questions +20, general community activity +15, social mentions +10, accepted feature requests +10. I was going to adopt it as-is for the Fenwright Guides program we're setting up. Is there anything wrong with it?
evals.expected_output: The quoted scale's implicit bet on reach named explicitly, its missing mentoring, tenure and coverage-gap lines pointed out, and an alternative weighting offered that puts answering questions above content creation, with every weight labelled self-set.
expectations: Names the disagreement explicitly as whether the program is buying reach or buying depth
Points out that the quoted scale ranks content creation highest
Points out that the quoted scale contains no mentoring line
Points out that the quoted scale contains no tenure or sustained-activity line
Points out that the quoted scale contains no coverage-gap line for region, language, vertical or ecosystem
Offers an alternative weighting that places answering other people's questions above content creation
Adds sustained tenure, mentoring and coverage gap as weighted signals in the alternative
Labels every weight it offers as self-set rather than an observed distribution
States that champion programs keep their internal scoring private, which is why no published distribution exists to calibrate against
Recommends recalibrating the weights to the program's stated purpose and writing that change into the charter rather than applying it silently

evals.prompt: Gallowbridge runs an open-source search product with a commercial edition. We have two engineers I can borrow for a quarter, and I want to build a contribution points system: every tracked contribution earns points, anyone can join, and points cash out. My plan is one global points table so it's fair to everyone, totals visible to our community team only so people don't get competitive about it, redemption as Amazon gift cards since that's what people actually want, and tracking in a shared spreadsheet to start. Poke holes in it.
evals.expected_output: Per-region point calibration, a published ledger, non-cash redemption, cycle-by-cycle weight revision with announcement, a budgeted portal instead of a spreadsheet, and explicit warnings about the archetype's irreversibility and compliance load.
expectations: Calibrates point values per region rather than using one global table
Gives the reason that contribution culture differs by market, so a single global table systematically under-recognises some regions
Publishes the ledger rather than keeping totals visible only to staff
Gives the governance reason for publishing: a private total only staff can see recreates the gatekeeper the ledger was meant to remove
Refuses cash or cash-equivalent redemption such as gift cards, and redirects redemption to training, certification and conference trips
Weights contributions by effort and current strategic need, treating the weighting as a steering wheel that over-rewards under-served areas until the imbalance closes
Revisits the weights every cycle and announces the change to members
Counts contribution types wider than code, naming at least talks, event organizing, content or forum answers
Rejects spreadsheet-based tracking at global scale and budgets a real portal as a known cost of this archetype rather than a surprise
Names the points ledger as the least reversible of the four archetypes, because stopping means honouring accrued balances
Flags the ledger's extra compliance load: published member activity records and redeemable value pull in gift limits, member tax exposure and a data review before launch
States that the ledger measures in order to award recognition and never functions as a quota whose miss triggers punishment

evals.prompt: Quillrun, we make a schema-migration CLI. We announce our community program Monday and I need the landing page copy today - can you just write it? The perks we've settled on are early access to release candidates, a private Slack channel with the team, and an invite to our annual summit. Name is Quillrun Navigators. Keep it punchy, I don't need a big strategy doc.
evals.expected_output: The landing-page-only request declined; a charter produced first covering the 12 questions with numbers marked sourced or self-set, validated section by section, and only then a public page limited to the publishable subset.
expectations: Refuses to hand back a perk list or landing page with no term, exit and bar attached
Produces the charter first and the public page second, in that order
Works through the 12 charter questions, covering at minimum purpose, archetype, criteria, obligations, perks, term, exit, compliance, operations and bar
Marks every number in the charter as sourced or self-set
Validates each section with the user before moving to the next rather than delivering the whole document in one pass

Limits the public page to purpose, criteria and anti-signals, obligations and the may-not list, perks, term dates with renewal and inactivity rules, alumni status, the disclosure expectation, and how to apply or be nominated
Keeps the candidate pipeline list, individual scores, budget per member, kill criteria and raw scorecard numbers internal
States that a charter with no named owner or budgeted monthly hours fails the readiness check, and says so instead of polishing the document
Does not treat the three named perks as a sufficient program design

evals.prompt: I maintain libcaldera, an open-source calendar-recurrence library. Solo maintainer, no company behind it, no money coming in beyond about $40/month in donations. There's a group of maybe 30 regulars in the GitHub discussions who are genuinely great. I want to name 25 of them libcaldera Champions. I can spare about 3 hours a month for this. I was thinking hoodies funded out of the donation pot, and a nice badge on their profile. Sound workable?
evals.expected_output: The 25-person cohort checked against 3 hours a month and cut down or shifted to a lower-touch archetype, swag replaced with standing and responsibility, the champion tier wired into the existing contributor ladder, and conduct and feedback-capacity gates raised.
expectations: Checks 25 champions against 3 hours a month using a figure of roughly 1-2 hours per champion per month and concludes the cohort far exceeds what those hours support
Labels the hours-per-champion figure as self-set, to be derived from the operating beats actually chosen
Recommends shrinking the cohort or moving to a lower-touch archetype rather than keeping 25
Recommends an invite-only circle as the default starting shape
States that for an open-source project with no vendor budget the currency is standing and responsibility, not swag
Connects the champion tier to the project's existing contributor ladder so recognition ladders into review rights and maintainership rather than sitting beside it
Keeps the emeritus or alumni exit that the contributor ladder already defines
Requires a code of conduct and a working moderation path to exist before the title is granted
Explains that a champion title grants implied authority, so granting it with no enforcement path is how a bad actor becomes an official one
Requires a named person who will actually receive and answer what champions raise, rather than a feedback obligation with no listener
